rst31-hygiene2-a001.title: Set wall-cleaning coverage by height and frequency
rst31-hygiene2-a001.text: The source’s facility-cleaning example includes daily cleaning of internal walls up to 1 m above the floor. Splashed residues readily remain on shelves and walls near preparation benches. Specify wall coverage on the checklist rather than stopping after wiping the visible floor. Treat wet-system floors after work and water or residues on dry-system floors when discovered. This is a source cleaning-plan example, not a statutory dimension common to every facility.

rst31-hygiene2-a002.title: Distinguish food-manufacturing water from everyday “drinkable water”
rst31-hygiene2-a002.text: The source’s food-manufacturing water refers to a water specification for producing particular foods. It includes tap water and water meeting the applicable food-manufacturing specification. Do not assume every well qualifies; ask facility management which standards and tests apply to the food produced. The everyday description “fit to drink” alone does not establish compliance with a specific food-manufacturing standard.

rst31-hygiene2-a003.title: Check water and equipment separately before work
rst31-hygiene2-a003.text: The operating example checks and records water condition at least once daily before work, and also checks drinking-well disinfection/purification equipment operation before work. Read the residual chlorine value of at least 0.1 ppm within that water/equipment’s management conditions. Do not guarantee food safety from one measurement alone; combine testing, tank cleaning and equipment inspection. Do not taste-test water with discolouration, turbidity, unusual odour or suspected disaster contamination. Confirm procedures appropriate to equipment categories and official guidance. Although the original lists taste among routine sensory checks, it does not instruct tasting water suspected to be abnormal or contaminated.

rst31-hygiene2-a004.title: Record health-harm information and refer it appropriately
rst31-hygiene2-a004.text: If several customers or a doctor report illness associated with the same food, a supplier announces an overseas-product recall, or self-testing of food eaten without heating detects harmful microorganisms, preserve the item, time, lot and communication details and have the responsible person consult the public health centre or relevant authority. Off-tastes/odours or mould from inadequate heating/packaging, and suspected metal or hard-resin contamination from machinery damage, also cannot be dismissed as harmless. Current implementing rules include a best-efforts information-provision provision for ordinary products; distinguish separate rules for relevant businesses handling Foods for Specified Health Uses or Foods with Function Claims. Do not turn old textbook wording into an identical penalty-backed notification duty for every case. Give consumers safe preparation/storage guidance and verified food information.

rst31-hygiene2-a005.title: Prepare for urgent allergy symptoms
rst31-hygiene2-a005.text: Food allergy can involve not only skin or digestive symptoms but urgent signs such as breathing difficulty, throat/chest tightness, extreme weakness or clouded consciousness. With urgent symptoms, staff should call 119 without waiting to diagnose or confirm the cause; do not make the guest stand or walk, and wait for emergency personnel there. Allocate calling, guiding responders and attending to other customers. Medication follows the guest’s prescription and official emergency procedures, not independently invented dosing instructions. Review official symptom charts and roles during training.

rst31-hygiene2-a006.title: Read the 2023 table separately from the 2026 system
rst31-hygiene2-a006.text: The original 2023 table lists eight mandatory items: shrimp, crab, wheat, buckwheat, egg, milk, peanut and walnut; its 20 recommended items include cashew and matsutake. It is a publication-period learning table. The Consumer Affairs Agency’s 1 April 2026 amendment moves cashew into specified mandatory ingredients, making nine, with a labelling transition until 31 March 2028. Pistachio is also added to recommended items, so do not rely only on the old item count when checking current ingredients. The system mainly covers packaged processed food and is not necessarily identical to restaurant-menu information. Check ingredients, seasonings and possible cross-contact without declaring unknowns safe. The 2023 recommended list is abalone, squid, salmon roe, orange, cashew, kiwi, beef, sesame, salmon, mackerel, soybean, chicken, banana, pork, matsutake, peach, yam, apple, gelatin and almond. The April 2026 recommended 20 remove cashew and matsutake and include macadamia and pistachio. Date comparisons with the old table and check actual ingredients against suppliers’ latest labels/specifications.

rst31-hygiene2-a007.title: Distinguish voluntary-recall notification cases and exclusions
rst31-hygiene2-a007.text: Voluntary-recall reporting informs authorities of a business recall of products violating or potentially violating the Food Sanitation Act; it differs from an administrative recall order. Review examples involving pathogens, composition-standard failures, additive-use violations, hard foreign objects or spoilage from defective packaging. Safety-labelling problems include undeclared wheat, an overstated use-by period or an improperly high storage-temperature statement. Small quantity alone does not establish exclusion. Consult the relevant office against legal conditions, such as clearly not being sold to an unspecified public and being readily recoverable, or clearly not being eaten by consumers. Do not omit stock or customer-hazard responses merely because a date has passed.

rst31-hygiene2-a008.title: Read temperature examples with their food categories
rst31-hygiene2-a008.text: The source gives examples of prepared meat/fish at 10℃ or below, raw-service seafood at 4℃ or below and fresh fruit/vegetables around 10℃. Finished-food storage examples are hot holding at 65℃ or above, a dedicated ambient-food case at 15–25℃, refrigeration at 10℃ or below and freezing at −15℃ or below. The 15–25℃ range does not authorise placing foods requiring refrigeration there; it illustrates a category suitable for ambient handling. Prioritise food-specific labels/characteristics and applicable store conditions. For stored unheated dishes, combine rapid cooling, refrigeration and covering and minimise time left in the source’s 10–60℃ danger zone.

rst31-hygiene2-a009.title: Read three-principle figures with their targets
rst31-hygiene2-a009.text: The original gives an example of infection from roughly 10–100 organisms, not a personally safe dose. Manage health, work clothing, footwear and handwashing to prevent introducing norovirus and similar hazards, and restrict dirty cardboard or foam materials too. The growth-prevention principle gives general storage examples of 10℃ or below or 60℃ or above, while post-cooking hot holding specifies 65℃ or above. For viruses that do not multiply in food, do not claim that refrigeration alone prevents contamination or infection.

rst31-hygiene2-a010.title: Separate dish pre-rinsing from detergent rinsing
rst31-hygiene2-a010.text: Remove food residues, pre-rinse with water or lukewarm water around 40℃, then remove dirt with suitable detergent. Rinse thoroughly afterwards and dry. The 40℃ figure is a working example, not a completed-disinfection temperature. Separately confirm the condition of at least 5 seconds under running water for dishes after detergent use; do not confuse it with pre-rinse temperature.

rst31-hygiene2-a011.title: Check handwashing layout and recontamination
rst31-hygiene2-a011.text: The source places handwashing facilities near each work-area entrance where splashes will not affect food and makes instructions easy to see. After washing, remove moisture with clean paper towels or similar material and dry thoroughly. If using alcohol disinfectant, follow the product method to cover fingertips and the whole hand. Do not just provide supplies: perform the washing and disposal movements to check that they do not contaminate hands or food.

rst31-hygiene2-a012.title: Small gaps around pipes can be entry points
rst31-hygiene2-a012.text: The source illustrates a roof rat passing through a gap of about 2 cm. Municipal pest guidance also calls for small-hole checks, but this is not a safe-gap limit; species, individuals and enlargement by gnawing vary. Inspect pipe penetrations, ceiling wiring and door/floor gaps, and discuss food-safe repairs with specialists. Do not ignore a gap merely because it is smaller than 2 cm.

rst31-hygiene2-a014.title: Distinguish sales-format labelling from hygiene controls
rst31-hygiene2-a014.text: The Consumer Affairs Agency’s labelling Q&A treats consumer processed food sold unpackaged or packed into a lunchbox on a customer’s order differently from prepackaged processed food. Separate provisions can still apply, including raw-beef warnings and business-use foods. Do not omit all labelling merely because sales are called “by weight”; confirm actual packaging and sales methods with the relevant office. Continue covering food and washing/disinfecting hands and utensils independently of labelling applicability.

rst31-hygiene2-a015.title: Read the 2003–2022 series on two axes
rst31-hygiene2-a015.text: Align the years on the horizontal axis, reading incidents on the incident scale and patients on the person scale. Equal visual heights of a line and bar do not mean equal quantities. The figures are 1585 incidents/29355 patients in 2003 and 962/6856 in 2022; annual patient counts from 2013 through 2022 are below 25000. From 2021 to 2022, incidents rise from 717 to 962 while patients fall from 11080 to 6856. Directions need not match. This historical national series does not show the latest situation or an individual store’s safety.

rst31-hygiene2-a016.title: Match inspection-form fields to evidence
rst31-hygiene2-a016.text: The reference form first identifies the facility, operator, location, business type, food/process features, HACCP approach, reference guide and hygiene lead. Then match the plan, necessary procedures, training, implementation records and periodic verification to actual evidence. General-hygiene fields cover responsibilities, premises, equipment, water, pest/rodent control, waste/drainage, handlers, retained samples and recalls. Critical-process fields follow hazard analysis, critical control points, limits, monitoring, deviation actions, verification and records. Finally check training attendance, incoming/outgoing goods, self-testing, notes, date and checker. Do not automatically award full marks for non-applicable items; verify the reason and remove them from the denominator. In an independent exercise, applicable items worth 6 and 4 score 6 and 0; a 2-point item is excluded, giving 6 out of 10 or 60%. These practice weights do not guarantee official inspection scoring or pass/fail criteria.

rst31-hygiene2-a017.title: Distinguish arrival time from eating time
rst31-hygiene2-a017.text: Delivery of cooked food must account for the time until customers actually eat, not just departure to arrival. A lunchbox may arrive on time but be eaten later because a meeting overruns; confirm temperature, storage and service conditions during that delay. Define pre-loading food temperatures and pre-cooling, in-transit temperature history and who controls food after arrival. Do not proceed unchanged with a plan that cannot maintain the specified conditions.

rst31-hygiene2-a018.title: The 2022 cause shares concern incidents
rst31-hygiene2-a018.text: The cause chart’s denominator is 962 incidents in 2022, not 6856 patients. Displayed shares are Anisakis 58.8%, Campylobacter 19.2%, norovirus 6.5%, plant natural toxins 3.5%, Salmonella 2.3%, Clostridium perfringens 2.3%, animal natural toxins 1.7%, staphylococci 1.6%, Kudoa 1.1%, unknown 0.9%, enterohaemorrhagic E. coli 0.8%, Bacillus cereus 0.3%, other 0.3%, other pathogenic E. coli 0.2%, chemicals 0.2% and other bacteria 0.1%. These are the chart’s rounded values and may not sum to exactly 100%. Even small categories require hazard assessment for the store’s menu and processes; do not exclude controls based on rank alone.

rst31-hygiene2-a019.title: Freezing effects depend on the hazard
rst31-hygiene2-a019.text: Appropriate freezing is effective against targeted parasites such as Anisakis, but confirm the organism, temperature and time. Do not claim that bacteria and viruses are universally killed too. The original’s destruction principle teaches combining suitable treatment such as heating with preventing recontamination and growth afterwards.

rst31-hygiene2-figure-cause-shares.caption: Read 2022 incident shares by cause on a common scale; these are not patient shares.
rst31-hygiene2-figure-cause-shares.alt: Read 2022 incident shares by cause on a common scale; these are not patient shares.

rst31-hygiene2-figure-historical-series.caption: An independent chart reads 2003–2022 incidents and patients on axes with different units.

rst31-hygiene2-figure-pipe-entry-gap.caption: Schematic inspection of gaps around a pipe. About 2 cm is a source guide example, not a safety boundary.
rst31-hygiene2-figure-pipe-entry-gap.alt: Schematic inspection of gaps around a pipe. About 2 cm is a source guide example, not a safety boundary.

rst31-hygiene2-figure-wall-cleaning-rang.caption: The source’s cleaning-plan example shows internal walls up to 1 m above the floor and splash-prone bench surroundings.
rst31-hygiene2-figure-wall-cleaning-rang.alt: The source’s cleaning-plan example shows internal walls up to 1 m above the floor and splash-prone bench surroundings.

rst31-hygiene2-figure-reference-form-exe.caption: An independent three-item exercise distinguishes the applicable-point denominator from points actually achieved.
rst31-hygiene2-figure-reference-form-exe.alt: An independent three-item exercise distinguishes the applicable-point denominator from points actually achieved.

rst31-hygiene2-q001.stem: Unused containers occupy the bench and finding needed tools takes too long. Which improvement fits the 5S distinctions?
rst31-hygiene2-q001.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when unused containers occupy the bench and tool searches take too long.
options: Separate removing unneeded items from setting fixed locations where required quantities can be retrieved
Omit habit-building education after one tidy-up
Treat surface disinfection as completing sorting and setting in order
Call removal of unnecessary items setting in order and set no locations
reasons: Sorting checks necessity and quantity; setting in order defines locations and retrieval. Cleaning, maintaining cleanliness and habit-building also continue separately.
Education and repetition needed to maintain cleanliness are missing.
Washing/disinfection alone does not sort necessity or quantity.
This reverses sorting and setting in order and leaves locations undefined.
rst31-hygiene2-q001.explanation: Sorting checks necessity and quantity; setting in order defines locations and retrieval. Cleaning, maintaining cleanliness and habit-building also continue separately.

rst31-hygiene2-q002.stem: A plan leaves the temperature checker and frequency blank. What makes it usable for implementation records?
rst31-hygiene2-q002.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when a plan omits temperature-check responsibilities and frequency.
options: Define the target, person, method and frequency and record measurements with deviation actions
Set only the form’s storage location and leave monitoring to individuals
Stop actual records once the critical step is selected
Estimate temperatures on verification day and backfill daily fields
reasons: Specify monitoring and connect the plan with implementation, deviations and corrective-action records.
Targets, responsibilities and frequency remain undefined.
A plan alone loses confirmation of implementation.
Later estimates are not actual monitoring records.
rst31-hygiene2-q002.explanation: Specify monitoring and connect the plan with implementation, deviations and corrective-action records.

rst31-hygiene2-q003.stem: What is appropriate when selecting a successor as food hygiene supervisor?
rst31-hygiene2-q003.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when selecting a successor as food hygiene supervisor.
options: Skip qualification documents if the person is head chef
Stop learning new information after appointment
Treat years of experience alone as equivalent to recognised training
Check listed qualifications or recognised course completion and plan practical refresher training for the business category
reasons: A job title does not replace checking recognised qualifications/training.
Plan continued learning after appointment.
Experience alone cannot establish appointment eligibility.
Check qualification requirements, roles and continued learning separately; titles and experience do not replace requirements.
rst31-hygiene2-q003.explanation: Check qualification requirements, roles and continued learning separately; titles and experience do not replace requirements.

rst31-hygiene2-q004.stem: The cleaning list says only “floor,” while the bench wall and underside of the drain cover are dirty. How should the source example be implemented?
rst31-hygiene2-q004.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when a floor-only list misses bench walls and drain-cover undersides.
options: Present the 1 m wall range as a universal legal dimension
Include daily internal-wall cleaning up to 1 m and remove the grating to wash the drain after floor cleaning
Leave water on dry-system floors until evening cleaning
Omit walls without visible dirt and wash only the cover top
reasons: This universalises the source example as law.
The 1 m is a source example specifying splash-prone walls. Remove the cover and residues from the drain, and immediately remove water from dry-system floors.
Remove water on dry-system floors when found.
This misses splashed walls and the cover underside.
rst31-hygiene2-q004.explanation: The 1 m is a source example specifying splash-prone walls. Remove the cover and residues from the drain, and immediately remove water from dry-system floors.

rst31-hygiene2-q005.stem: Hood oil, cabinet-fan dust and freezer frost are all left untreated as the same “dirt.” Which explanation is correct?
rst31-hygiene2-q005.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when oil, dust and frost are treated as one neglected problem.
options: Thicker frost always improves cooling
Oil is only cosmetic and never affects ventilation
Oil/dust affect fire and ventilation risks, while frost reduces cooling efficiency, so inspect by part
Cold kills every microorganism, so the cabinet needs no cleaning
reasons: Thick frost lowers cooling efficiency.
Oil and dust also affect ventilation and fire.
Effects on fire, ventilation and cooling differ as well as hygiene; clean and inspect each part appropriately.
Microorganisms can survive low temperatures.
rst31-hygiene2-q005.explanation: Effects on fire, ventilation and cooling differ as well as hygiene; clean and inspect each part appropriately.

rst31-hygiene2-q006.stem: Lighting is dim and packaging is stored on the warehouse floor. Which cleaning/check combination is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q006.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when lighting is dim and packaging sits directly on the floor.
options: Sweep only because dimness does not affect foreign-object detection
Wet powered lights and put packaging on the floor to keep it cool
Switch lighting power off, clean suitably for its materials and store packaging off the floor
Clean only the floor and omit temperature/humidity and vents
reasons: Dimness obstructs foreign-object detection.
Wetting powered equipment and floor-storing packaging are inappropriate.
Check safe lighting cleaning and brightness alongside floor storage, temperature/humidity and vents.
Check temperature/humidity, high areas and vents too.
rst31-hygiene2-q006.explanation: Check safe lighting cleaning and brightness alongside floor storage, temperature/humidity and vents.

rst31-hygiene2-q007.stem: A store has an animal-interaction seating area, and a worker returns to the kitchen after toilet cleaning. Which plan is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q007.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when returning from toilet cleaning to a kitchen in an animal-interaction store.
options: Separate kitchen and animal areas and use toilet-only tools in a sequence that limits contamination spread
Use the toilet-seat cloth on taps and then in the kitchen
Leave the delivery door permanently open after unloading for ventilation
Allow animals in food stores because they are permitted in seating areas
reasons: Separate animal/customer and food zones and manage toilet tools, sequence and entrances separately.
The dirty cloth spreads contamination to cleaner areas.
Consider closure outside delivery times and necessary screens.
Animal seating permission is not permission for food areas.
rst31-hygiene2-q007.explanation: Separate animal/customer and food zones and manage toilet tools, sequence and entrances separately.

rst31-hygiene2-q008.stem: Dirt remains in board scratches and strainer rims. What improvement is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q008.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when board scratches and strainer rims retain dirt.
options: Dry with detergent still on, without rinsing
Keep torn mesh because residues fall through easily
Scrub scratches, backs/sides, mesh and rim undersides and replace weakened mesh
Wash only visible flat surfaces and apply disinfectant alone to scratches
reasons: Thorough detergent rinsing is required.
Torn mesh can detach and become foreign material.
Wash dirt-retaining scratches and undersides and replace detachable mesh to prevent foreign objects.
Dirt removal and blind-spot cleaning are missing.
rst31-hygiene2-q008.explanation: Wash dirt-retaining scratches and undersides and replace detachable mesh to prevent foreign objects.

rst31-hygiene2-q009.stem: Machine parts, the sink overflow and wet sponges were missed in checks. What should be included?
rst31-hygiene2-q009.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when machine parts, sink overflows and wet sponges are overlooked.
options: Store sponges permanently submerged in the sink bottom
Exclude small metal-scourer fragments from foreign-object checks
Wash only machine exteriors and the sink centre
Wash removable parts, overflows and drain traps, and wash/disinfect/dry sponges
reasons: Leaving sponges wet permits growth.
Metal fragments can be hazardous foreign objects.
Exterior/centre cleaning alone misses hidden residues.
Removable parts, blind spots and tools themselves can cause contamination or foreign objects; avoid leaving sponges wet.
rst31-hygiene2-q009.explanation: Removable parts, blind spots and tools themselves can cause contamination or foreign objects; avoid leaving sponges wet.

rst31-hygiene2-q010.stem: In training on neutral, alkaline and acidic cleaners, which combination is correct?
rst31-hygiene2-q010.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when classifying neutral, alkaline and acidic cleaners.
options: Scale is grease, so neutral cleaner always removes it
All dish soaps are neutral regardless of product
Use alkaline cleaner bare-handed because eye protection is unnecessary
Consider neutral cleaner for ordinary food soil, suitable alkali for heavy grease/burnt deposits, and suitable acid for scale
reasons: Scale mainly comes from water minerals.
Some dish soaps are mildly alkaline.
Check hand and eye protection for alkaline products.
Select for soil, material and product directions. Some dish soaps are mildly alkaline, and alkaline cleaners need protective equipment.
rst31-hygiene2-q010.explanation: Select for soil, material and product directions. Some dish soaps are mildly alkaline, and alkaline cleaners need protective equipment.

rst31-hygiene2-q011.stem: Which ingredient examples match the source’s acidic-cleaner classification?
rst31-hygiene2-q011.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when checking acidic-cleaner ingredient examples.
options: Sodium and potassium hydroxide are both organic acids
Malic/citric acids are organic; hydrochloric/nitric acids are inorganic
Mixing acid with sodium hypochlorite makes it safer
Anionic surfactants mainly disinfect every pathogen
reasons: Sodium hydroxide and similar products are alkalis.
Distinguish ingredient class from purpose. Mixing acids and chlorine is dangerous; detergent does not replace disinfectant.
Mixing acidic and chlorine products can release harmful gas.
This treats detergent as a universal germicide.
rst31-hygiene2-q011.explanation: Distinguish ingredient class from purpose. Mixing acids and chlorine is dangerous; detergent does not replace disinfectant.

rst31-hygiene2-q012.stem: Metal tools receive chlorine treatment after washing and a refrigerator is cleaned. Which point is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q012.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when treating washed metal tools with chlorine and cleaning refrigeration.
options: Follow product-specified after-treatment and remove food/shelves to treat interiors and handles
Leave food inside and spray only around it
A wetter bench always strengthens alcohol disinfection by dilution
Leave a thick chlorine residue without wiping to prevent corrosion
reasons: Follow material/product after-treatment. Protect/remove food and shelves, treat interiors/handles and watch alcohol dilution by moisture.
Food is unprotected and cleaning blind spots remain.
Water dilutes alcohol and can reduce effectiveness.
This ignores corrosion-related residues and specified after-treatment.
rst31-hygiene2-q012.explanation: Follow material/product after-treatment. Protect/remove food and shelves, treat interiors/handles and watch alcohol dilution by moisture.

rst31-hygiene2-q013.stem: Which storage arrangement after disinfection is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q013.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when choosing storage after disinfection.
options: Use a machine with missing screws once its door is shut
Hang cleaning tools over clean dishes to drain
Invert large bowls after drying, check machine screws and hang cleaning tools in a separate area
Stack bowls wet to slow drying
reasons: Missing-part foreign objects and machine condition remain unchecked.
Drips from cleaning tools contaminate clean equipment.
Use item-specific drying/missing-part checks and storage preventing recontamination; hanging positions must not affect food.
Moisture remaining at the bottom is unhygienic.
rst31-hygiene2-q013.explanation: Use item-specific drying/missing-part checks and storage preventing recontamination; hanging positions must not affect food.

rst31-hygiene2-q014.stem: Which improvement to handwashing supplies and layout is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q014.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when improving handwashing supplies and layout.
options: Provide splash-limiting space, touch-free water, clean paper towels and a bin
Omit paper towels and facility cleaning if soap is present
Share one nailbrush to avoid disinfecting it
Aim reflected dryer airflow at finished food to dry it too
reasons: Both usability and recontamination prevention matter; check dryer interiors/airflow and nailbrush controls too.
Supplies, clean facilities and drying remain necessary.
A shared brush can become a secondary contamination source.
This airflow layout can spread contamination to food.
rst31-hygiene2-q014.explanation: Both usability and recontamination prevention matter; check dryer interiors/airflow and nailbrush controls too.

rst31-hygiene2-q015.stem: A new worker assumes any well water qualifies as food-manufacturing water. What correction is needed?
rst31-hygiene2-q015.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when a new worker treats all well water as food-manufacturing water.
options: Check the production standard for the food and the water’s compliance
Call any clear well water food-manufacturing water
Omit every specific manufacturing-standard check for tap water
Use the term only for utensil-washing water
reasons: It is a specification category for particular food production, not compliance determined by appearance or name.
Clarity alone does not establish compliance.
This skips the target food’s manufacturing-standard check.
This wrongly narrows the production-water category.
rst31-hygiene2-q015.explanation: It is a specification category for particular food production, not compliance determined by appearance or name.

rst31-hygiene2-q016.stem: How should the source’s start-of-work checks be incorporated into a plan?
rst31-hygiene2-q016.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when turning start-of-work checks into a plan.
options: Have everyone taste unusual-smelling water before deciding to stop use
Combine daily checks and annual water testing as one task
Check water condition at least once daily before work and record equipment operation/residual chlorine separately
Omit post-disaster water testing whenever residual chlorine is normal
reasons: Do not drink suspected contaminated water to test it.
Daily checks and periodic tests are distinct controls.
Routine condition, equipment operation and water testing are separate checks; do not taste water suspected abnormal or contaminated.
One measurement cannot rule out disaster contamination.
rst31-hygiene2-q016.explanation: Routine condition, equipment operation and water testing are separate checks; do not taste water suspected abnormal or contaminated.

rst31-hygiene2-q017.stem: Small flies appear in drains and large flies near the delivery entrance. What investigation is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q017.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when small drain flies and larger entrance flies appear.
options: Separate internal breeding from outside entry and inspect drains/covers, doors and screens
Assume all come from outside and ignore drains
Treat leftover alcohol and food refuse as non-sources despite odours
Assume sticky traps always require spraying near food
reasons: Distinguish habitats and entry routes and inspect vegetation, refuse and leftover drinks; do not rely on spraying near food.
This misses breeding in drains.
Odours and residues from drinks and refuse can attract or support pests.
This relies on spraying next to food.
rst31-hygiene2-q017.explanation: Distinguish habitats and entry routes and inspect vegetation, refuse and leftover drinks; do not rely on spraying near food.

rst31-hygiene2-q018.stem: Before commissioning a pest/rodent specialist, which priority locations should be identified?
rst31-hygiene2-q018.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when prioritising locations for a specialist pest survey.
options: Inspect warm equipment, damp waste paper outdoors and pipe/ceiling gaps according to species and routes
Exclude warm machinery because German cockroaches avoid it
Treat sticky traps and poison bait as identical, with no food-protection checks
Ignore ceilings because roof rats climb poorly
reasons: Use species-specific habitats/movement and select trapping, repellence or chemicals with food impacts in mind.
Warm equipment is a priority habitat for German cockroaches.
Trapping and chemicals differ in action and food impact.
Roof rats are good at vertical movement.
rst31-hygiene2-q018.explanation: Use species-specific habitats/movement and select trapping, repellence or chemicals with food impacts in mind.

rst31-hygiene2-q019.stem: Waste and drainage procedures are being reviewed. Which combination is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q019.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when reviewing waste and drainage procedures.
options: Mix bottles/cans still containing contents with food waste
Discharge wastewater directly onto the kitchen floor to dry naturally
Drain and seal food waste, specify collection arrangements and route wastewater into pipes/equipment
Stop checking bin interiors and lids after collection
reasons: Contents remain and separation conditions are not followed.
Dirty water spreads over floors and clean areas.
Manage segregation, sealing, collection, bin hygiene and drainage routes as a connected system.
Residues inside bins and lids can be pest sources.
rst31-hygiene2-q019.explanation: Manage segregation, sealing, collection, bin hygiene and drainage routes as a connected system.

rst31-hygiene2-q020.stem: Which items should be added to start-of-work health and clothing checks?
rst31-hygiene2-q020.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when completing start-of-work health and clothing checks.
options: Do not report infected wounds if there is no abdominal pain
Report jaundice, pus and discharge too and inspect torn clothing, hair under caps and changing areas
Skip checks for protruding hair once a cap is worn
Omit all later symptom checks after a stool test
reasons: Infected wounds also affect health and task decisions.
Checks go beyond digestive symptoms; damaged clothing, hair and changing areas also affect contamination prevention.
Check protruding hair during work too.
Testing does not rule out later illness or infection.
rst31-hygiene2-q020.explanation: Checks go beyond digestive symptoms; damaged clothing, hair and changing areas also affect contamination prevention.

rst31-hygiene2-q021.stem: Which sequence/control is appropriate for hand wounds and gloves?
rst31-hygiene2-q021.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when checking hand injuries and glove use.
options: Wear the same shoes between toilets and kitchen without zoning
Put gloves on before removing rings/watches and tape over tears
Dry removed single-use gloves for reuse by the same person
Report the wound, obtain a task decision, wash hands and use specified waterproof covering and suitable gloves
reasons: Footwear can carry contamination from toilets to the kitchen.
Prepare before washing and replace torn gloves.
Do not reuse single-use gloves.
Remove washing obstructions and confirm task suitability/protection; do not spread contamination through glove reuse or cross-zone footwear.
rst31-hygiene2-q021.explanation: Remove washing obstructions and confirm task suitability/protection; do not spread contamination through glove reuse or cross-zone footwear.

rst31-hygiene2-q022.stem: A hard-resin machine part is chipped and may have entered food. How should information be handled?
rst31-hygiene2-q022.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when a hard-resin fragment may have contaminated food.
options: Automatically dismiss harm if the fragment is small
Preserve item/time/lot information and have the supervisor consult public health authorities
Discard all records and wait until illness is confirmed
Do not tell the store about foreign-product recalls because they are overseas
reasons: Fragment size alone cannot rule out harm.
Retain foreign-object, recall and testing information that may involve harm and refer it appropriately; preserve and consult before certainty.
This loses investigative evidence and delays action.
Share recall information relevant to the store’s products.
rst31-hygiene2-q022.explanation: Retain foreign-object, recall and testing information that may involve harm and refer it appropriately; preserve and consult before certainty.

rst31-hygiene2-q023.stem: After eating, a guest has breathing difficulty and clouded consciousness. What initial response is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q023.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when a guest develops breathing difficulty and clouded consciousness after eating.
options: Rule out a severe reaction because little was eaten
Wait for ingredient confirmation and send the guest walking home without calling
Treat the symptoms as urgent, call 119 and wait for responders without making the guest stand or walk
Independently administer a new unprescribed medicine
reasons: Severe allergy can follow small amounts.
This delays emergency help and makes the guest walk.
Severe symptoms require emergency help without waiting for cause confirmation; do not independently diagnose, medicate or encourage walking.
Staff must not independently decide on medication.
rst31-hygiene2-q023.explanation: Severe symptoms require emergency help without waiting for cause confirmation; do not independently diagnose, medicate or encourage walking.

rst31-hygiene2-q024.stem: Someone uses only the 2023 table to check labels in October 2026. Which explanation is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q024.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when using a 2023 table for October 2026 labelling checks.
options: Check official updates on mandatory cashew status, transition and recommended pistachio inclusion
Treat the eight 2023 items as an unchanged current list forever
Claim no transition exists after the 2026 amendment date
Always treat packaged labels and restaurant-menu information as the same system
reasons: Distinguish the April 2026 amendment from transition through March 2028 and check the system applying to the food.
This omits the amended cashew classification.
This ignores the transition period.
This ignores differences in products and sales formats.
rst31-hygiene2-q024.explanation: Distinguish the April 2026 amendment from transition through March 2028 and check the system applying to the food.

rst31-hygiene2-q025.stem: What information is appropriate when consulting on whether to notify a voluntary recall?
rst31-hygiene2-q025.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when consulting on voluntary-recall notification applicability.
options: Exempt small quantities regardless of potential harm
Omit applicability and hazard responses once the date has passed
Treat every voluntary recall as an administrative order
Organise hard-object/safety-label problems and applicability conditions such as customers and recoverability
reasons: Small quantity alone does not establish exemption.
This confuses notification conditions with customer-hazard responses.
A voluntary recall differs from an administrative order.
Check reporting and exclusion conditions against law; possible exclusion does not justify omitting hazard/customer responses.
rst31-hygiene2-q025.explanation: Check reporting and exclusion conditions against law; possible exclusion does not justify omitting hazard/customer responses.

rst31-hygiene2-q026.stem: Temperature-controlled lunchboxes will be eaten after arrival. Which plan is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q026.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when delivered lunchboxes require temperature control until later eating.
options: Reuse a container that carried non-food yesterday based only on appearance
Exclude post-arrival waiting from the plan
Consider necessary pre-cooling, rapid loading/unloading, in-transit temperature/humidity and time until eating
Check only arrival time, not loading temperature
reasons: Previous cargo can transfer contamination.
Time until eating also affects safety.
Track departure, transit, arrival and eating conditions and prevent contamination from vehicles, containers and mixed cargo.
Food temperature control begins at loading.
rst31-hygiene2-q026.explanation: Track departure, transit, arrival and eating conditions and prevent contamination from vehicles, containers and mixed cargo.

rst31-hygiene2-q027.stem: How should delivery lots, display cases and bulk sales be checked?
rst31-hygiene2-q027.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when checking incoming lots, display cases and sales by weight.
options: Use FIFO alone without dates or lot identification
Lower the setting if the load limit is exceeded and stop checking
Set acceptance/deviation records, observe loading/temperature limits and maintain covers/tool hygiene for bulk sales
Exempt bulk-sale hand hygiene because labelling differs
reasons: Expiry and lot identification are needed alongside receipt order.
Overloading obstructs cold-air circulation.
Quantity, dates, display, temperature and hygiene are distinct controls; labelling scope is not a hygiene exemption.
Labelling treatment and hygiene controls are separate.
rst31-hygiene2-q027.explanation: Quantity, dates, display, temperature and hygiene are distinct controls; labelling scope is not a hygiene exemption.

rst31-hygiene2-q028.stem: Hygiene training for experienced staff is being reviewed. What is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q028.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when reviewing hygiene-training content and effectiveness including experienced staff.
options: Use actual store items to check health reporting, clothing, handwashing, tool zoning and chemicals and verify behaviour
Omit store-specific zoning and chemicals for experienced staff
Skip demonstrations/review once attendance is signed
Exclude chemicals because they are separate from cooking
reasons: Use role-appropriate content and updated material, checking behaviour as well as understanding to improve training.
This misses education suited to the store’s equipment, zones and chemicals.
Attendance alone does not establish practical competence.
Chemical-related food contamination also requires training.
rst31-hygiene2-q028.explanation: Use role-appropriate content and updated material, checking behaviour as well as understanding to improve training.

rst31-hygiene2-q029.stem: Records repeatedly show the same cooling delay. How should they be used?
rst31-hygiene2-q029.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when the same cooling delay recurs in records.
options: Assume stored forms remove any need for improvement
Erase abnormal fields to explain safety to customers
Keep only normal days to identify trends
Organise lot/destination traceability, improve equipment/work and compare later records
reasons: Use records for operational improvement and verification.
Erasing facts prevents traceability and improvement.
Abnormality trends and causes become unreadable.
Use records to detect warning signs, trace products, improve efficiency and explain verified performance; forms alone do not guarantee safety.
rst31-hygiene2-q029.explanation: Use records to detect warning signs, trace products, improve efficiency and explain verified performance; forms alone do not guarantee safety.

rst31-hygiene2-q030.stem: The source’s “ambient foods at 15–25℃” is being applied to cold salad. Which judgement is correct?
rst31-hygiene2-q030.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when applying an ambient 15–25℃ example to cold salad.
options: Equate freezing at−15℃ with retained-sample conditions
Store every cooked food at 15–25℃
Check the category and refrigerate cold dishes appropriately rather than substituting the ambient example
Unify raw-service seafood and cooking ingredients by appearance alone
reasons: Retained samples have separate targets and storage conditions.
This extends an ambient-food example to refrigerated food.
Read temperature with food/process categories and prioritise labels/specified conditions; do not extend ambient examples to chilled food.
Appearance alone does not establish raw-service categories.
rst31-hygiene2-q030.explanation: Read temperature with food/process categories and prioritise labels/specified conditions; do not extend ambient examples to chilled food.

rst31-hygiene2-q031.stem: Which plan is correct for keeping a cooked stew until the next day?
rst31-hygiene2-q031.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when planning overnight storage of cooked stew.
options: Reaching 100℃ kills every spore, so omit cooling
Use the 65℃ hot-holding condition as a refrigeration maximum
Use 10℃ within 30 minutes or 20℃ within 60 minutes as the large-scale cooling example
Check centre temperature/holding time and cool promptly for appropriate storage because spores may remain
reasons: Spores can survive ordinary cooking.
65℃ here is a hot-holding condition.
The example’s temperatures and times are reversed.
Heating may not remove every hazard; use appropriate cooling/storage and do not reverse the large-scale example’s times and temperatures.
rst31-hygiene2-q031.explanation: Heating may not remove every hazard; use appropriate cooling/storage and do not reverse the large-scale example’s times and temperatures.

rst31-hygiene2-q032.stem: Which workflow is appropriate for plating an unheated vegetable dish?
rst31-hygiene2-q032.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when plating unheated dressed vegetables.
options: Use a raw-meat bench once vegetables have been washed
Wash, apply any necessary suitable treatment and rinse; use clean gloves/tools after handwashing, then cover and refrigerate
Dispose of rubbish wearing mixing gloves and return to plating in them
Replace torn gloves without checking fragments
reasons: This transfers contamination to food without later heating.
Unheated food cannot rely on a later cook: link ingredient treatment, recontamination prevention, glove replacement/fragment checks, covering and refrigeration.
Change contaminated gloves and wash hands.
Also check whether fragments entered the food.
rst31-hygiene2-q032.explanation: Unheated food cannot rely on a later cook: link ingredient treatment, recontamination prevention, glove replacement/fragment checks, covering and refrigeration.

rst31-hygiene2-q033.stem: What is central when explaining the Food Sanitation Act’s purpose in training?
rst31-hygiene2-q033.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when explaining the Food Sanitation Act’s purpose.
options: Prevent food-related sanitary hazards and protect health
Shorten cooking time and reduce staff
Standardise food-sales rankings
Make dishes taste identical at all stores
reasons: The purpose is sanitary-hazard prevention and health protection, distinct from efficiency, sales or uniform taste.
Efficiency is not itself the law’s hazard-prevention purpose.
It is not a system for uniform sales rankings.
Uniform flavour is not its purpose.
rst31-hygiene2-q033.explanation: The purpose is sanitary-hazard prevention and health protection, distinct from efficiency, sales or uniform taste.

rst31-hygiene2-q034.stem: Which target/condition pairing matches the source’s heat-disinfection example?
rst31-hygiene2-q034.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when matching objects to heat-disinfection conditions.
options: Transfer the 75℃/1 minute food-centre condition directly to every utensil
Suitable washed utensils:80℃ for at least 5 minutes; boiling examples for heat-resistant parts/cloths:100℃ for at least 5 minutes
Treat every utensil at 100℃ regardless of heat resistance
Ignore contact time once 80℃ is reached
reasons: Food heating and utensil disinfection have different targets.
Utensil and food conditions differ; examples require suitability for material, shape, equipment and facility procedures.
Check heat resistance and material.
Check temperature together with holding time.
rst31-hygiene2-q034.explanation: Utensil and food conditions differ; examples require suitability for material, shape, equipment and facility procedures.

rst31-hygiene2-q035.stem: A receiving tank’s water source and capacity are being checked. Which interpretation fits the source categories?
rst31-hygiene2-q035.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when checking a receiving tank’s source and capacity.
options: Classify a well-water tank as a simplified dedicated water supply by capacity alone
Even with tap water as the sole source, distinguish simplified dedicated supplies over 10 m³ from smaller equipment
Claim 100-person or 20 m³/day conditions have no exceptions
Classify dedicated supplies solely by whether a tank exists
reasons: This overlooks the source-water condition for the simplified category.
Combine source, effective capacity and supply conditions; legal exceptions require confirmation with management.
Legal exceptions also need checking.
Dedicated-supply classification depends on supply and other conditions.
rst31-hygiene2-q035.explanation: Combine source, effective capacity and supply conditions; legal exceptions require confirmation with management.

rst31-hygiene2-q036.stem: Old and current rules on off-taste information for ordinary foods are compared. Which explanation is correct?
rst31-hygiene2-q036.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when comparing old/current off-taste information rules for ordinary foods.
options: Claim identical notification duties and penalties for every food complaint
Ignore doctors’ reports because they are not customers
Ignore potential harm whenever the general rule is best efforts
Distinguish general best-efforts information provisions from special-food rules and record/consult on possible harm
reasons: Rules differ for ordinary and specified products.
Collect doctors’ information too and refer it appropriately.
Best efforts does not mean potential harm may be ignored.
Do not confuse covered products, actions or obligation levels; gather and consult on safety information.
rst31-hygiene2-q036.explanation: Do not confuse covered products, actions or obligation levels; gather and consult on safety information.

rst31-hygiene2-q037.stem: Which combination matches large-scale cooking temperature/time guides?
rst31-hygiene2-q037.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when checking large-scale cooking temperature/time guides.
options: Use 50℃ at the centre even for potentially norovirus-contaminated bivalves
Treat 20℃ after 60 minutes cooling as the same guide
An instant at 75℃ always meets the condition
Ordinary heating:75℃ centre for at least 1 minute; cooling:around 20℃ within 30 minutes or 10℃ within 60 minutes; hot holding:at least 65℃
reasons: This does not meet the norovirus heating conditions.
Cooling temperatures and times are mismatched.
Holding time is needed as well as temperature.
Check centre temperature and holding time and distinguish norovirus heating, cooling and hot-holding conditions.
rst31-hygiene2-q037.explanation: Check centre temperature and holding time and distinguish norovirus heating, cooling and hot-holding conditions.

rst31-hygiene2-q038.stem: How should an old allergen table be used alongside guest information?
rst31-hygiene2-q038.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when reading an old allergen table for service explanations.
options: Removing an ingredient always removes shared-equipment cross-contact
Distinguish the publication-year table from current official coverage and check ingredients, seasonings and unintended cross-contact
Nothing recommended in 2023 can ever become mandatory
Different packaged/restaurant rules remove any need to inform guests
reasons: Ingredient removal alone cannot eliminate cross-contact.
Check both system year/scope and operational cross-contact; do not freeze old categories or make vague safety guarantees.
Food labelling systems can be amended.
Different systems do not remove efforts to share verified information.
rst31-hygiene2-q038.explanation: Check both system year/scope and operational cross-contact; do not freeze old categories or make vague safety guarantees.

rst31-hygiene2-q039.stem: Training compares a general 60℃ storage example with 65℃ post-cooking hot holding. Which explanation is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q039.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when distinguishing general 60℃ storage from 65℃ hot holding.
options: Omit handwashing because viruses do not grow in chilled food
Read them as different target/process conditions and confirm that cold alone does not prevent viral contamination
Treat the 10–100-organism infection example as a safe consumption limit
Call 60℃ versus 65℃ a tolerance and use only the lower value everywhere
reasons: Cold alone does not prevent viral contamination.
Do not confuse general principles and specific processes; a low infectious-dose example is not a safe dose.
This turns an infection guide into a safety allowance.
This replaces process-specific conditions with the lower value.
rst31-hygiene2-q039.explanation: Do not confuse general principles and specific processes; a low infectious-dose example is not a safe dose.

rst31-hygiene2-q040.stem: Which combination improves facility cleaning and shared-machine procedures?
rst31-hygiene2-q040.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when organising facility cleaning and shared-machine procedures.
options: Copy another store’s procedure including its personnel names
Use untreated raw-meat tools for cooked food if no dedicated machine exists
Omit used-cloth treatment on facility-cleaning days
Specify the store’s targets/methods and washing, disinfection, drying and storage when switching uses
reasons: This does not check local equipment, responsibilities or feasibility.
It transfers raw-meat contamination to cooked food.
Used tools require separate controls despite facility cleaning.
Set workable facility-specific procedures and prevent secondary contamination from shared equipment and used tools.
rst31-hygiene2-q040.explanation: Set workable facility-specific procedures and prevent secondary contamination from shared equipment and used tools.

rst31-hygiene2-q041.stem: Dishes were pre-rinsed at about 40℃ under the example. What judgement follows?
rst31-hygiene2-q041.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when using about 40℃ water for dish pre-rinsing.
options: Warm water replaces detergent, so skip dirt checks
Correct pre-rinse temperature removes detergent-rinsing checks
40℃ pre-rinsing equals 80℃/5 minute heat disinfection
Pre-rinsing is not completed disinfection; continue detergent washing, thorough rinsing and drying
reasons: Pre-rinsing alone does not confirm dirt removal.
Pre-rinse temperature and detergent-rinsing conditions differ.
This wrongly substitutes pre-rinsing for disinfection requirements.
Check the distinct purposes/conditions of pre-rinsing, washing, rinsing, necessary disinfection and drying.
rst31-hygiene2-q041.explanation: Check the distinct purposes/conditions of pre-rinsing, washing, rinsing, necessary disinfection and drying.

rst31-hygiene2-q042.stem: Handwashing is moved near an entrance. Which layout/use check is appropriate?
rst31-hygiene2-q042.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when moving handwashing near an entrance.
options: Assume wet hands concentrate alcohol
Check food-safe splash positioning and instructions, then dry after washing before suitable disinfection
Skip actual usability once a sign exists
Accept splashes directly above food as long as the entrance is near
reasons: Moisture on hands dilutes alcohol.
Combine access flow, food impact, instructions, drying and product conditions.
Check recontamination through actual use movements.
The layout must prevent splashes onto food.
rst31-hygiene2-q042.explanation: Combine access flow, food impact, instructions, drying and product conditions.

rst31-hygiene2-q043.stem: There is about a 2 cm gap between pipe and wall. How should source/municipal guides be used?
rst31-hygiene2-q043.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when finding an approximately 2 cm pipe gap.
options: Ignore it unconditionally because rats look larger
Inspect/consult on repair as a possible entry and do not declare smaller gaps safe
Guarantee no species passes through less than 2 cm
Exclude ceiling gaps because rats cannot move vertically
reasons: This ignores passage through small openings.
The guide warns about small entry points, not a maximum safe gap; check pipes and ceilings too.
Species/individuals vary, so it is not an absolute safety boundary.
Roof rats are good at vertical movement.
rst31-hygiene2-q043.explanation: The guide warns about small entry points, not a maximum safe gap; check pipes and ceilings too.

rst31-hygiene2-q044.stem: Hot greasy wastewater and cleaning-chemical wastewater need treatment. What should be checked?
rst31-hygiene2-q044.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when handling hot oily and cleaning-chemical wastewater.
options: Ignore acidity/alkalinity and grease after cooling
Treat clarity as proof of water-quality compliance
Check temperature, acidity/alkalinity, organics, sediment, fats, equipment and local standards
Choose any facility standard when discharging to public sewers
reasons: Other wastewater properties can matter besides temperature.
Appearance does not establish composition or compliance.
Temperature is not the only issue; treat according to sewer and municipal conditions.
Check applicable sewer and local standards.
rst31-hygiene2-q044.explanation: Temperature is not the only issue; treat according to sewer and municipal conditions.

rst31-hygiene2-q045.stem: Historical national data show 717 incidents/11080 patients in 2021 and 962/6856 in 2022. Which reading is correct?
rst31-hygiene2-q045.objective: Distinguish source conditions from operational controls when reading 2021 figures 717/11080 and 2022 figures 962/6856.
options: Add incidents and patients as the same unit to decide change
Present 2022 as this year’s latest figures
Incidents rose and patients fell, so they did not move in the same direction
Patients must have risen because incidents rose
reasons: Incidents and people cannot be added as one unit.
This replaces the current year with historical figures.
Incidents and patients are different indicators whose directions may differ; identify the years.
The stated patient count fell.
rst31-hygiene2-q045.explanation: Incidents and patients are different indicators whose directions may differ; identify the years.

rst31-hygiene2-q046.stem: In an independent inspection-form exercise, two applicable items worth 6 and 4 score 6 and 0. A separate 2-point item is non-applicable. What is the exercise score rate?
rst31-hygiene2-q046.objective: Distinguish form evidence and the score denominator excluding non-applicable items.
options: 60%:6 scored out of 10 applicable points
50%:include the non-applicable item in the denominator
80%:add full points for the excluded item only to the numerator
100%:records give full marks even for unmet items
reasons: Excluding the item gives 6+4=10 available and 6+0=6 scored, or 60%.
This includes the excluded 2 points in the denominator.
Do not add excluded items to the numerator.
Records and actual compliance are different.
rst31-hygiene2-q046.explanation: Calculate with the question’s independent weights. Check real inspection applicability, weighting and exclusions under the responsible criteria; do not equate them with app mock-exam scores.

rst31-hygiene2-q047.stem: Using a reference inspection form, how should initial facility information and later management fields be handled?
rst31-hygiene2-q047.objective: Match identifying form fields to management evidence.
options: Omit abnormalities/actions from notes because notes do not directly score points
Omit critical-process monitoring/deviation actions if general-hygiene records exist
Change only another store’s name and skip guide/supervisor checks
Confirm facility name/management approach and compare plans, procedures, training, records and verification with actual evidence
reasons: Abnormalities and responses are important evidence of implementation.
General hygiene and critical processes work together.
Facility correspondence with guidance/responsibilities is unverified.
Match facility identity to evidence supporting management fields.
rst31-hygiene2-q047.explanation: Do more than fill a form: compare the facility’s approach/responsibilities with actual records/work. Do not turn reference-form scores into app pass/fail results.

rst31-hygiene2-q048.stem: A delivered food’s outer box is dirty. Which control prevents contamination being brought into the kitchen?
rst31-hygiene2-q048.objective: Apply the introduction-prevention principle to delivery packaging.
options: Store chilled food in its box because dirt cannot transfer when cold
Keep dirty outer packaging out of work zones and transfer food hygienically in a designated area under store procedures
Place the box on a preparation bench and clean around it after unpacking
Switch to foam to omit dirt checks and enter any zone
reasons: Cold storage does not eliminate contamination transfer from the outer box.
Restrict dirty packaging and transfer food hygienically to prevent introduction.
Bringing it to the bench can contaminate surroundings before unpacking.
Packaging material alone does not establish cleanliness or entry permission.
rst31-hygiene2-q048.explanation: Restrict dirty cardboard/foam and confirm transfer procedures that protect food and clean work areas.
